Cyclic Hexagon

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Six dots sit on one circle and make two triangles; see how three distances across one triangle multiply to exactly the same number as three distances back the other way.
How to play: Drag any dot around the circle, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names or the extra circles, and press Reset to put the dots back.
Look for the math

Six points on one circle can be read as two interlaced triangles. Drop a perpendicular from each corner of one triangle to the opposite side of the other. The three lengths you get on one side, multiplied together, always equal the three on the other side — even when the points are in a strange order around the circle.

Three lengths, two products

Name the corners A0, A1, A2 and B0, B1, B2, counting the small index around in a loop. From Ai we drop a perpendicular to the line joining Bi-1 and Bi+1, and call that length ki. From Bi we drop one to Ai-1Ai+1, and call that length li. The page's claim is

k0 · k1 · k2 = l0 · l1 · l2

Drag the dots: the two numbers under the picture change all the time, but they stay equal. The logic test checks this on 3,000 different arrangements, including orders that make a crossed, non-convex hexagon, and no exception turned up.

Why a side gives the answer

Here is the useful fact. If P is on a circumcircle of diameter D and U, V are two more points on it, then the triangle PUV has a right angle at the foot of the perpendicular from P to UV. Comparing areas gives

dist(P, line UV) = |PU| · |PV| / D

Apply this with P = Ai, U = Bi-1, V = Bi+1, then do the same with the letters swapped. Multiply the three results for each family and every chord of the hexagon appears exactly once:

∏ ki = ∏ li = (a0 · a1 · a2 · a3 · a4 · a5) / D³

Here a0 through a5 are the six sides of the alternating hexagon and D is the circle's diameter. That is the page's formula (4), also confirmed over the same 3,000 arrangements. Near a coincidence of two vertices the applet's own drawing code snaps the perpendicular foot to the vertex; the formula is meant for distinct vertices.

The circles in the proof

Tick “circles on sides”: each side of the hexagon becomes the diameter of a circle, so its radius is half that side. Tick “circles on radii”: each vertex carries a copy of the big circle shrunk by a homothety of factor one half, radius R/2. Two circles that meet in a chord of length c and have radii r1 and r2 obey the page's lemma

c = r1 · r2 / R′

where R′ is the circumradius of the triangle formed by the two circle centres and one meeting point; the test checks this lemma on 600 pairs of circles. One detail of the page is worth flagging: its intermediate formula (2) prints Pi+1 and Qi+1, but with the indices used here the correct partners for ki and li are Qi-1 and Pi-1. As printed it fails in almost every configuration; shifted by one it is exact. The final products (1), (3) and (4) are unaffected, because a product does not care which way round the indices run.

More than six points

The same idea needs no convexity: the six dots may sit on the circle in any order, so the picture is really a statement about two triangles sharing a circle. It also works for two n-gons on one circle with n at least 3: multiply the distances from every corner of one n-gon to the line through its two neighbours in the other n-gon, and you get the product for the other direction. The check runs 500 arrangements each for n = 4 and n = 5, and the equality and the corresponding side formula hold there too.

Try this: put A0 almost on top of B1, then pull it away. Watch the products dip towards zero and climb back, staying equal the whole time.
